name: Dog domestication, Late Pleistocene Eurasia
summary: Dogs were living with Late Pleistocene foragers in Europe by about 12,200 BCE, when a sick young dog, probably nursed by people, was buried with two humans at Bonn-Oberkassel.
description: Domestic dogs are first described with reasonable certainty from Magdalenian sites in western Europe; claims for older Aurignacian dogs are contentious. At Bonn-Oberkassel, Germany, a dog about 27 to 28 weeks old was buried with two adult humans in what is the oldest known dog burial, and its bones date to about 12,290-12,050 cal BCE. Lines in its tooth enamel point to repeated grave illness that it is unlikely to have survived without human care.

impact.note: Scored on the general view, not on the cited paper, that later dogs descend from Late Pleistocene Eurasian domestication and came to live with people on every inhabited continent; a hunting, guarding and hauling partner was a new capability, and a few later lines such as herding and sled dogs built on it.

date.label: c. 12,290-12,050 BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Four radiocarbon dates on the bones of the Bonn-Oberkassel dog fall between about 12,900 and 11,850 cal BCE, with a weighted mean between 12,290 and 12,050 cal BCE.

evidence.supports: Four radiocarbon dates were performed on the canine bones (for details see Table 3), situating them between ca. 12900/12850 and ca. 11900/11850 cal BC. Their weighted mean is between 12290 and 12050 cal BC

date.label: c. 12,290-12,050 BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: The authors call the two dogs of the Bonn-Oberkassel burial some of the oldest undisputed evidence for domestic dogs; the date given here is that of the younger dog, from the dating section, not from this passage.

evidence.supports: These two late Pleistocene Bonn-Oberkassel dogs provide some of the oldest undisputed evidence for domestic dogs.

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: Table 2 of the source gives approximate dates for other Magdalenian dogs, some older than Bonn-Oberkassel (Monruz and Hauterive-Champréveyres about 13,500 cal BC, Erralla possibly older); their original reports were not read.
The Aurignacian dog claims (Goyet, Předmostí), which the lead's 'possibly c. 21,000 BCE' rests on, were not checked and are called contentious in the source read.
Genetic estimates of when and where dogs split from wolves (for example Perri 2021, Bergström 2020) were not read; they bear on the place and on the reach score.

research.note: No accepted domestic dogs are older than the Magdalenian group of western Europe: the source calls the Bonn-Oberkassel dogs some of the oldest undisputed evidence for domestic dogs and their burial the oldest known, lists the other Magdalenian dogs beside them, and calls older Aurignacian claims contentious. Where wolves were first domesticated is not settled by it.
